newsitem.title: LATVIA: LATVIA-IMF SAYS BUDGET DEFICIT MAY PRESENT WORRIES.
newsitem.headline: LATVIA-IMF SAYS BUDGET DEFICIT MAY PRESENT WORRIES.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) said on Friday that Latvia's looming budget deficit was no cause for concern unless it signified a relaxation of the tight fiscal policies credited with stabilising the economy.

Finance Minister Robert Zile said on Thursday that the country's original goal of a balanced 1997 budget was in jeopardy as income tax revenues would probably fall short of target and additional expenditures were in the pipeline.
Zile said the deficit could reach around 10 million lats or 0.4 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
"It (the impact of the deficit) depends on the circumstances," Dimitri Demekas, the IMF's resident representative in Latvia and Estonia, told Reuters.
"If it stems from an unexpected but manageble set of circumstances it is one thing," he said.
"But if it stems from a relaxation of policy...that would not be a positive development," he said.
The government of outgoing Prime Minister Andris Shkele had previously set a balanced budget as a firm policy goal.
"We are well aware that expenditures have been building up," Demekas added.
He said special care had to be taken ahead of the 1998 autumn elections, when politicians may be tempted to boost their popularity through increased spending.
A balanced budget was seen as one of the crowning achievements of Shkele's time in office.
Shkele, who quit on Monday after he fell out with the governing parties, is credited with successfully pushing tough austerity measures through the fractious 100-seat parliament.
New Prime Minister Guntar Krasts, the economy minister under Shkele, has said he wants to push on with economic reforms.
